name: Rifat Erdem Sahin
tagline: Turkish roots, a US exchange year, two tries at university, 40+ contracts across 8 countries, and one habit: learning in public. From tutoring to AI, now helping others make the same jump.
belief: I'm passionate about being early to disruption, retooling people for it, and helping them become Delivery Pilots. AI is raising the skills bar faster than any school can keep up, and the people who do well will be the ones who can teach themselves. I've been doing that my whole life.

chapters.title: Growing up in Turkey: life was all about exams
chapters.text: I grew up in Turkey, with roots that go further back: my DNA traces to Mongolia, and in history class I learned about the Ottoman Empire and how many cultures it joined together. Growing up there was all about studying for exams. Everything hung on one score. We moved from Ankara to Istanbul, and my sister graduated top of her class as valedictorian. Even then I watched and read more in English than in Turkish. The internet was my second classroom.

chapters.title: Exchange student at an American high school
chapters.text: Then I went to the USA as an exchange student and finished high school in America. I was living in a new language and a new culture, and nobody there knew me. I learned early how to adapt, and how to pick up whatever the next room expected of me.

chapters.title: Civil Engineering, not Computer Science
chapters.text: The exam decided where I went, and it wasn't Computer Science, the place I wanted. I ended up in Civil Engineering instead. I tried to finish university twice, and each time it was one of two things: I wasn't interested in what I was studying, or I was far too interested in computers, going deep on what fascinated me instead of what the syllabus asked. Looking back, that's where my real education started: without the certificate, I had to prove what I could do by doing it.

chapters.title: Learning became the job
chapters.text: So I taught myself, and I still do, every day. I build things to learn them, write everything down (my notes vault is past 46,000 notes), and treat my CV as code: something I keep improving and shipping. Self-learning isn't a side habit for me. It's how I built a career.

chapters.title: Ten years in Britain, home in Cambridge
chapters.text: Then I moved to Britain and started again as an immigrant. I chose the UK for two reasons: a lower level of corruption (it ranks far better on the Corruption Perceptions Index), and a language I'd already been living in, since I'd consumed most of my content in English for years. My sister made the same kind of move, to France. I've lived in the UK for 10 years now, at home in Cambridge, raising my two daughters here. I'm still learning every day, right now the UK tax system. It's the same lesson again: what you can learn and show matters more than where you started.

chapters.title: Delivering across borders
chapters.text: Work took me around the world, mostly on business: the USA, Switzerland, Germany, France, Turkey, Cyprus, England and Scotland. I've delivered more than 40 contracts. Every country taught me the same thing: delivery is about people as much as tech.

chapters.title: Three rounds of business
chapters.text: I started in business early. My first business ran from 18 to 28, then I stopped. From 38 to 48 I built and ran a second one, which I'm now taking through liquidation. Closing a company is a lesson most founders never talk about. Now I'm on round three: Delivery Pilot. Everything from the first two rounds, what worked, what didn't and what it costs, goes into this one.

chapters.title: Working in tech, teaching what I learn
chapters.text: Today I work in tech (I work at IBM) on onboarding and reliability, getting customers live safely, on time, with real money depending on it. Alongside that I make videos, run a Skool community and a cohort, and share everything I learn in the open.

chapters.title: AI is raising the bar, so I'm opening the story
chapters.text: AI is moving fast, and the skills employers expect are rising with it. Entry-level roles are shrinking, and the jobs that remain ask for judgment, specs and delivery, not just typing code. I'm telling my story openly because someone without a degree, without the 'right' start, can still get into the cockpit. That's what the Delivery Pilot course is for, and it's free for students.

values.title: Early to the disruption
values.text: See the shift before it lands, and move first: from tutoring to real estate to DevOps to AI.

values.title: Retool people
values.text: Nobody gets left behind. Give people the skills, the tools and the courage to move up a seat.

values.title: Self-learning first
values.text: No one is coming to teach you the next tool. Learn it, build it, show it.

values.title: Open by default
values.text: My notes, code and mistakes are public, so others can skip the expensive parts.

values.title: Honest about AI
values.text: Not hype, not doom. Here's what the data says and what to do about it.

values.title: Lift people up a seat
values.text: Riders become drivers, and drivers become Delivery Pilots. Nobody gets left behind.
